summary: This document describes requirements, architecture and solutions for protecting point-to-point services in a ring of MPLS Transport Profile nodes. It defines a Ring Protection Switching protocol so traffic can be quickly steered around a failure, meeting the ring protection requirements of RFC 5654.

eli5.summary: Picture cars driving around a circular road. If part of the road is blocked, they turn around and go the other way round the circle to still reach their destination.

subtitle: How a ring of MPLS-TP nodes shares protection tunnels and uses the RPS protocol to steer traffic around a failure.

tldr.problem: MPLS-TP networks are often built as rings, and operators need fast recovery (sub 50 ms) from link and node failures without running a protection instance for every path.
tldr.mechanism: Each egress node gets working and protection ring tunnels in both directions. Traffic is carried inside them and moved to the protection tunnel by wrapping, short-wrapping or steering. A single Ring Protection Switching (RPS) protocol instance per ring node, sent in-band on the G-ACh, coordinates the nodes.
tldr.outcome: Protection effort depends on the ring size and not on the number of protected LSPs, and no control-plane interaction is needed during a switch. The RFC covers point-to-point services only.

facts.label: RPS timing
facts.value: 3.3 ms for the first three, then 5 seconds

today: RFC 8227 is a Proposed Standard from August 2017, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines MSRP and the RPS protocol for point-to-point services on MPLS-TP rings.

sections.title: Why Rings Need Their Own Protection
sections.content:
Several service providers asked for MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) to work in ring topologies with a high level of survivability, as described in Section 2.5.6.1 of RFC 5654. The introduction notes that MPLS-TP networks are often built as rings, which calls for a protection mechanism that is simple to operate and recovers in under 50 ms.

RFC 8227 specifies MPLS-TP Shared-Ring Protection (MSRP) for point-to-point transport paths. Point-to-multipoint paths are out of scope. It also defines the Ring Protection Switching (RPS) protocol used to coordinate the nodes.

Section 3 checks the design against the ring criteria. Each ring node needs only one RPS instance per ring, regardless of how many LSPs are protected. The number of ring tunnel labels depends on the number of ring nodes, not on the number of protected LSPs. A switch uses in-band RPS and OAM messages, so no control-plane interaction is required.
sections.eli5: Many telephone networks are laid out in circles. This RFC gives circles of equipment a simple way to keep working if one piece breaks, quickly and without a lot of paperwork.

sections.title: Ring Tunnels and Labels
sections.content:
MSRP adds a logical layer of ring tunnels that act as a server layer for the LSPs crossing the ring. Once the tunnels exist, forwarding and protection switching on the ring happen at the tunnel level. A port can carry several ring tunnels, and a tunnel can carry several LSPs. The label stack is [Ring Tunnel Label|LSP Label|Service Label](Payload).

Ring tunnels are built per egress node. LSPs that leave the ring at the same node and travel the same direction share tunnels. For each egress node, four tunnels are established: a clockwise working tunnel protected by an anticlockwise protection tunnel, and an anticlockwise working tunnel protected by a clockwise protection tunnel. The notation is R<d><p><X>, so RcW_D is the clockwise working tunnel to Node D and RaP_D is the anticlockwise protection tunnel to Node D.

Ring tunnel labels are downstream-assigned (RFC 3031) and can be configured statically, provisioned by a controller or distributed by a control protocol. The control plane for label distribution is outside the scope.

On forwarding, the ingress node pushes the working ring tunnel label, transit nodes swap it, and the egress node pops it and forwards on the inner LSP and service labels.
sections.eli5: Think of lanes painted around a roundabout, one set for each exit. Cars heading for the same exit share a lane, and there is a backup lane running the opposite way around.

sections.title: Failure Detection and the Three Protection Modes
sections.content:
Failures are found with MPLS-TP section-layer OAM (RFC 6371). The two ports of a link form a Maintenance Entity Group, with a MEP in each ring port. Continuity Check packets are exchanged periodically, and three consecutive lost CC packets MUST be interpreted as a link failure. A node failure is treated as the failure of the two links attached to it.

Every node keeps a ring map: the nodes in the ring, their adjacency, and whether each link is Intact or Severed. All nodes on a ring MUST use the same one of three protection mechanisms:

  • Wrapping: both nodes next to the failure switch. Traffic goes onto the protection tunnel upstream of the failure, travels around the ring, and switches back to the working tunnel downstream to reach the egress. The protection tunnel is a closed ring.
  • Short-wrapping: only the node upstream of the failure switches. The protection tunnel ends at the egress node, so the traffic leaves the ring from it. This cuts the detour, but the two directions of a bidirectional LSP are no longer co-routed.
  • Steering: the node that detects the failure sends RPS requests along the ring. Each ingress node checks its ring map and, if its LSPs are affected, moves them from the working to the protection tunnel; the egress node drops traffic from the protection tunnel.

If an RPS message shows a mode that was not provisioned in a node, a failure of protocol is reported and the protection mechanism is not activated. If the egress node itself fails, ingress nodes learn from RPS messages that it is unreachable and send nothing, which avoids a traffic loop.
sections.eli5: Neighbors keep saying hello to each other. If three hellos in a row go missing, they decide the road between them is broken, and the cars turn around or pick the other way depending on the ring's rule.

sections.title: Interconnected Rings
sections.content:
Two typical shapes are described. In single-node interconnected rings the rings meet at one node, which is a single point of failure, so the RFC says this topology should be avoided in real transport networks. In dual-node interconnected rings two nodes belong to both rings, so one interconnection node can fail and service can still recover.

The RPS protocol runs on each ring independently, and a failure in one ring only triggers switching in that ring unless it is on the interconnection node. LSPs are stitched at the interconnection node: the source ring's tunnel label is popped, the LSP label is swapped, and the destination ring's tunnel label is pushed.

In the dual-node case the two nodes can be managed as a virtual node group. Each ring SHOULD get working and protection ring tunnels to that group, and the same LSP label is assigned on both nodes for each traversing LSP. The working tunnel direction SHOULD be the same on both rings. Interconnection nodes use the ring map and fault location to decide whether a destination is still reachable; if not, the LSP MUST switch to the protection tunnel and cross at the other interconnection node.
sections.eli5: When two roundabouts touch, cars switch from one to the other at the shared exits. With two shared exits, traffic can use the second one if the first is blocked.

sections.title: The RPS Message
sections.content:
RPS processes in ring nodes MUST communicate over the Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh). Each node has a node ID that MUST be unique on the ring, with valid values 1 to 127, and the protocol supports at most 127 nodes on a ring. The message carries a Destination Node ID, a Source Node ID, an 8-bit Request code and a 2-bit M field for the protection mode: 01 wrapping, 10 short-wrapping and 11 steering (00 is reserved).

The destination node ID is always the adjacent node on the far side of the failure. IANA allocated G-ACh channel type 0x002A for RPS and created the MPLS RPS Request Code Registry, with allocations by Specification Required.

When nothing is wrong, each node periodically sends a No Request (NR) to both neighbors. After a change, the first three messages are sent as fast as possible; for switching within 50 ms their interval SHOULD be 3.3 ms, and later messages SHOULD be sent every 5 seconds. A node that is not the destination forwards the message immediately.

RFC 8227 explains why a new protocol was defined instead of reusing PSC (RFC 6378, RFC 6974). On a ring of N nodes, PSC needs (N-1) instances and (N-1) * 2 MEPs on every node, while RPS needs one instance and 2 MEPs per node.
sections.eli5: The nodes pass short notes around the ring. Each note says who it is for, who sent it, and what is wrong, using a small code number so every node reads it the same way.

sections.title: RPS Requests, States and Priorities
sections.content:
Requests have a priority order, highest first: Lockout of Protection (LP), Forced Switch (FS), Signal Fail (SF), Manual Switch (MS), Wait-to-Restore (WTR), Exercise (EXER), Reverse Request (RR) and No Request (NR). Higher-priority requests preempt lower ones, and a failure of the RPS protocol or controller MUST NOT trigger a switch. Operators can issue LP, FS, MS and EXER commands through the management system. SF is raised automatically by OAM, and WTR when the failure clears. The WTR time can be set from 0 to 12 minutes in 1 minute steps, with a default of 5 minutes. Clear and Lockout of Working are not carried by RPS.

A node is in one of three RPS states:

  • Idle: no requests, sending and receiving NR, and the protection tunnels are blocked.
  • Switching: it initiated or is the destination of a request, and it terminates received requests instead of forwarding them.
  • Pass-through: its highest request is neither from nor for it, so it relays requests unchanged and enables traffic on the protection tunnels.

For a unidirectional failure, the destination node replies with RR on the short path and the received code on the long path. The ring can hold several switches at once, which segments it into separate parts. Multiple MS requests on different links with no higher request cause no switch and existing switches are dropped.
sections.eli5: Each worker is either calm, busy fixing something, or just passing messages along. Important messages beat less important ones, and a worker waits a few minutes after a repair before trusting the road again.

sections.title: Choosing a Mode
sections.content: Only one protection mode can be provisioned in the whole ring. Wrapping works for point-to-point LSPs and for point-to-multipoint uses, keeps bidirectional traffic co-routed, and has the largest extra delay and bandwidth use. Short-wrapping and steering protect only point-to-point LSPs. Short-wrapping reduces delay and bandwidth compared with wrapping, but the two directions are not totally co-routed. Steering has the least delay and bandwidth use of the three, and can keep the two directions co-routed.
sections.eli5: The ring has to pick one rule for everybody. A safe-but-long detour, a shorter detour, or switching at the start of the trip each trade off distance against fuss.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
MPLS-TP builds on the MPLS security model (RFC 5920). If an attacker injects or modifies RPS messages, ring nodes might disagree on the protection action, and improper switching could briefly break services. RPS should therefore be used within a trusted MPLS-TP network domain (RFC 6941).

RPS depends on the security of the G-ACh. As with RFC 6378, the G-ACh is connection oriented, so injection needs subversion of a transit node, which is hard to prevent at the protocol level; management-level techniques are more appropriate.
sections.eli5: If a stranger could pass fake notes around the ring, the workers might send cars the wrong way for a while. So the ring should only be used inside a network its owners trust.
